report.answer_text:
What ToolShell was
On July 19, 2025, Microsoft confirmed that a zero-day affecting on-premises SharePoint Servers was being actively exploited. Researcher Khoa Dinh named it "ToolShell".[1] It was assigned CVE-2025-53770, with a related bypass tracked as CVE-2025-53771.[1]
CVE-2025-53770 is a critical remote code execution flaw with a CVSS score of 9.8[2]. It stems from a deserialization issue in a legacy SharePoint endpoint (ToolPane.aspx). Attackers can use it to execute arbitrary code without authentication.[3]
CVE-2025-53771 is a spoofing flaw (CVSS 6.5) that allows an authentication bypass through header spoofing[4].
The chain is a patch bypass. CVE-2025-53770 is a direct variant of CVE-2025-49706, which Microsoft tried to fix in the July 2025 Patch Tuesday roll-up.[2]
Attackers could deploy web shells, harvest machine keys, and maintain persistent access[5]. That is why patching alone didn't evict them. Compromised servers also needed key rotation and a hunt for leftover access.
Affected products
Only on-premises SharePoint is affected. That means SharePoint Server Subscription Edition, 2019 and 2016. SharePoint 2010 and 2013 are end-of-life but are still listed by Microsoft as affected.[2]
SharePoint Online and Microsoft 365 are not affected.[3]
Who was hit
Sectors: Reported sectors include education, finance, government, healthcare, energy, telecom, and enterprise environments.[6] SentinelOne saw early exploitation against high-value targets, mainly technology consulting, manufacturing, critical infrastructure, and professional services tied to sensitive architecture and engineering.[1]
U.S. federal agencies: Confirmed victims include U.S. federal agencies, universities, energy firms, and telecoms.[3]
Scale: Bloomberg reported on July 23 that there were over 400 victims.[7] Estimates varied by source and date. Bitsight cited 75-85+ servers globally[6] early on.
Attribution and later findings: Hackers believed to be associated with China used the flaw against government agencies, universities, telecom providers, and finance organizations.[8] Symantec later reported victims including a Middle East telecom provider, government bodies in Africa, South America and the Middle East, a U.S. university, and a European finance company[8]. It said a larger set of Chinese threat actors exploited the flaw than was previously known[8]. SOCRadar also reported that Warlock ransomware was deployed via ToolShell exploits[9].
Response
Microsoft issued an emergency out-of-band security update on July 19, 2025[2]. CISA added CVE-2025-53770 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on July 20.[9]
